abstract: |
  When several variables are observed over the same hierarchy, such as worker admissions and dismissals recorded by region, it seems natural to reconcile their forecasts jointly so that cross-variable dependence can inform the adjustment. We show when this helps. Minimum trace reconciliation can be read as a regression of the base forecast errors on the observed incoherences. In that form, joint reconciliation coincides with reconciling each variable separately if and only if each variable's separately reconciled errors are uncorrelated with the other variables' incoherences. Separable error covariances, and dependence confined to the coherent part of the errors, are special cases, so in a common simulation design joint reconciliation has no population advantage. We propose two effect sizes and a likelihood ratio test for real data. In simulations the gains are modest even when the error covariance is known, and with an estimated covariance joint reconciliation can lose accuracy at small sample sizes because it must estimate cross-variable covariances. For monthly Brazilian employment data over 2007--2019, the test detects a small departure, and with ARIMA base forecasts joint reconciliation does not systematically improve the forecasts of either variable. It does improve forecasts of net employment change, reducing the national mean squared error by `r targets::tar_read(numbers)$appNetPointTotal`%, consistent with the fact that with the true covariance minimum trace reconciliation is optimal for every linear combination of the series, not just on average. For probabilistic forecasts of net change, modelling the dependence between the variables' base forecasts matters most.
